
# introduction

# Introduction

Aegis is a systems-oriented programming language under active development. It
targets a specific contradiction in modern tooling: LLM-assisted programming
benefits from fluent, invisible abstractions, while systems programming demands
explicit control. Aegis responds with a **deliberately tiny grammar** so that
both humans and models can hold the entire language in one context window.

## Principles

- **Stack-by-default memory.** The compiler allocates on the stack and only
  introduces automatic reference counting (ARC) where data provably escapes
  the current frame. No `Box`/`Rc` spellings: escape is inferred.
- **Errors are values.** There is no `try`/`catch`/`throw`. Functions return
  `Result[T, E]`; the compiler rejects code that ignores an unhandled
  `Result` or `Option`.
- **Design by contract.** `requires` / `ensures` / `old(...)` annotate the
  edges of every function and check them at runtime; the state machine support
  turns "which state is this domain object in" into a compile-checked fact.
- **Concurrency as actors.** No mutexes. Structs communicate via `emit` events
  and `on` handlers. Values are never silently shared between execution
  contexts.
- **Composition, not inheritance.** Data lives in `struct`, behavior in
  `impl`. No `class`, no `extends`.

## Status

Aegis is a working compiler today: you can write structs, contracts, state
machines, event loops, closures, and higher-order list operations, and compile
them to native executables. See [Quickstart](quickstart.md) to install Aegis
and run your first program, and [Roadmap](roadmap.md) for where it is heading.

# language/grammar

# Grammar & keywords

## Keywords

Aegis keeps its keyword list small on purpose (context efficiency). The full
set is:

```
struct  impl  fn  loop  while  break  continue
if  else  match  in  state
trait  for  pub  extern  after
let  mut  const  import
requires  ensures  old
emit  on  transition
return  ok  err  some  none
enum
true  false
```

`@module` tags attach a domain namespace to a file (used by the cross-file
`import` path of the spec). Programs without module tags are simple: parse a
file, validate it, emit it.

## Identifiers

An identifier is a letter or `_`, followed by letters, digits, or `_`
(`[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*`). `state` and `transition` are recognized
contextually rather than lexed as keywords, but avoid reusing them as names.

## Operators

Highest precedence to lowest:

| Level | Operators |
| --- | --- |
| unary | `-` (numeric negate), `!` (Bool not), `~` (bitwise not) |
| power | `**` (right-associative) |
| multiplicative | `*` `/` `%` |
| additive | `+` `-` |
| shift | `<<` `>>` |
| comparison | `<` `<=` `>` `>=` |
| equality | `==` `!=` |
| bitwise and | `&` |
| bitwise xor | `^` |
| bitwise or | `\|` |
| logical and (short-circuit) | `&&` |
| logical or (short-circuit) | `\|\|` |

The `&` `|` `^` `~` `<<` `>>` operators are integer-only (natively sized
`i8..u64` or `Int`) and width-exact: bare literals adopt the other operand's
width (same rule as arithmetic), and mixed widths without an explicit
conversion are rejected. Precedence follows C/Rust, so equality binds looser
than `&` — a mask comparison needs parentheses, as in C: `(attrs & 3) == 1`.
A prefix `|` in expression position opens a lambda head (`|x: Int| x * 2`),
never bitwise-or; a match-arm `|` still forms alternatives
(`Kind::Int(n) | Kind::Str(s) => ...`).

`+` also concatenates `Str`, and `==`/`!=` compare strings by content. `**`
is the power operator (`a ** b` desugars to `a.pow(b)`; right-associative,
so `2 ** 3 ** 2` is `2 ** (3 ** 2)`, and `-2 ** 2` is `-(2 ** 2)`). There is
no `++`/`--` (use `+= 1`). Compound assignment `+= -= *= /= %= <<= >>= &= ^=
|=` is supported, each desugaring to a read-modify-write of the same target.

## Top-level items

A source file is a sequence of top-level items:

```
state OrderState { Pending, Paid, Shipped }   // state machine
struct BankAccount { owner: String, mut balance: Int }
struct Box[T] { mut value: T }                // generic struct with type parameter
trait Greeter {                                // method set + contract spec
    requires self.energy > 0
    fn greet(self, name: String) -> String     // declaration, no body
}
impl Greeter for Loud {                        // trait impl
    requires self.energy > 0
    fn greet(self, name: String) -> String { ... }
}
impl BankAccount {
    fn deposit(mut self, amount: Int) -> Empty { ... }
}
struct Order { }
impl Order @ OrderState::Pending {             // state-guarded impl
    fn process_payment(mut self) { ... }
}
```

## Generic structs

Structs can have type parameters, enabling reusable data structures:

```
struct Box[T] {
    mut value: T
}

struct Pair[A, B] {
    first: A,
    second: B
}
```

Instantiate generic structs with concrete type arguments:

```
let int_box = Box[Int] { value: 42 }
let str_box = Box[String] { value: "hello" }
let pair = Pair[Int, String] { first: 1, second: "one" }
```

Generics are instantiated per concrete type: `Box[Int]` is a struct with
`value: Int`, and `Box[String]` is a separate struct with `value: String`.

## Generic methods

Methods can declare their own type parameters, independent of the receiver:

```
impl Util {
    fn identity[T](self, x: T) -> T {
        return x
    }
    fn first[T](self, xs: List[T]) -> T {
        return xs[0]
    }
}
```

Call them with explicit type arguments that ride inside the method name:

```
let v = u.identity[Int](42)
let head = u.first[String](["a", "b", "c"])
let nested = u.identity[List[Int]](xs)
```

A generic method is instantiated per distinct call-site type instantiation,
substituting the type parameters in the parameters, return type, and `let`
annotations. Calling with the wrong number of type arguments (or none at all)
errors with `no method '<name>' on type <Receiver>`.

## Multi-line literals

Struct, list and map literals may span lines. Newlines are allowed between
elements, after commas (a trailing comma before the closing delimiter is fine),
and right after the opening delimiter:

```
let p = Point {
    x: 3,
    y: 4,
}
let xs = [
    1,
    2,
    3,
]
let m = {
    "a": 1,
    "b": 2,
}
```

The block-vs-literal disambiguation is unaffected: `if flag { ... }` still opens
a block (never a struct initializer), because control-flow heads are parsed with
struct-init suppressed. The canonical formatter still prints literals on a
single line.

## Visibility

Structs and fields can be marked as `pub` (public) or left private (default):

```
pub struct PublicBox {
    pub mut value: Int
}

struct PrivateBox {
    mut value: Int
}
```

Public items are accessible from other modules. Private items are only
accessible within their own module. Visibility is enforced at compile time:

- A struct is usable from another module only if declared `pub struct`. Private
  structs can be named, constructed (`Struct { ... }`), field-accessed and
  method-called only inside their own module.
- Inside a `pub` struct, a field is readable/writable from another module only
  if declared `pub` (or `pub mut`). Private fields stay within their module.
- Methods inherit the receiver struct's visibility: a `pub` struct's methods
  are callable cross-module; a private struct's methods are not.
- Same-module access never requires `pub`.

A module is the namespace introduced by the nearest preceding `@module <name>`
tag; items before any tag belong to the root module. `import @<name>` records a
dependency on a module that must exist somewhere in the compiled files.

## Multi-file compilation

The compiler accepts multiple source files and builds a single program from
them:

```bash
aegis lib.aegis main.aegis --main Main::run --emit-exe main
```

All items from all input files are available to each other. This enables
building programs from multiple modules without explicit import statements.

## Archive linking

A compiled program can be packaged into a library archive and later linked into
an executable, so builds can split into a library step and an app link step:

```bash
aegis lib.aegis app.aegis --main App::run --emit-archive app.a
aegis app.a --emit-exe app
```

Object and archive files (`*.o`, `*.obj`, `*.a`, `*.lib`) can be passed directly
to `--emit-exe`: when every input is a compiled artifact the compiler links them
with the runtime. Like `--emit-exe`, `--emit-archive` resolves the entry point
from `--main` or the default `impl X { fn main(self) }` method, so an archive
produced this way links into a running executable.

## Single-command FFI linking

Sources and compiled artifacts can be mixed in one invocation, so FFI builds
never need a manual clang step:

```bash
aegis app.aegis helper.c --main App::run --emit-exe app
aegis app.aegis helper.o libapp.a --emit-exe app
```

The compiler parses the `.aegis` files and passes the object/archive/C inputs
straight to the final link, where a `.c` input is compiled at the link step.
Mixing is only allowed with `--emit-exe`; compiling objects alone (or on their
own with `--emit-obj`) is a usage error. `-l <name>`/`-l<name>` and
`-L <dir>`/`-L<dir>` pass through to the link (as clang `-l`/`-L`):

```bash
aegis app.aegis --main App::run -L lib/generated -l helpers --emit-exe app
```

Archives are found by name (`-l helpers` locates `helpers.lib` on COFF or
`libhelpers.a` on ELF). A search dir alone does not link anything — archives
are only pulled in when named by a `-l`, exactly like gcc/clang.

## Foreign Function Interface (FFI)

Aegis can call C functions using `extern "C"` declarations:

```
extern "C" fn add_numbers(a: Int, b: Int) -> Int
extern "C" fn multiply(a: Int, b: Int) -> Int

struct Suite { }

impl Suite {
    fn run(self) -> Int {
        let sum = add_numbers(10, 20)
        let product = multiply(5, 7)
        return 0
    }
}
```

The extern function must be implemented in C and linked at compile time.
Parameters and return types must be primitive types (Int, Float, Bool, String)
or sized widths or [opaque handles](#opaque-handles). A parameter may instead be
declared `out name: T` — `T*` on the C side: the callee writes a result into a
slot Aegis allocates, and a call passes `out name` to claim it (see
[Out params](../language/types.md#out-params-i3)).

A `-> Str` return is a C `char*` that is at best transient - valid only until
the callee's next call. Aegis copies it into an owned String the moment the
call returns, and a NULL C string reads back as `""`; an `out msg: Str`
readback is copied the same way (see [C-string marshaling](../language/types.md#c-string-marshaling-i4)).

### Opaque handles

A C library that hands back a pointer it owns - a `FILE*`, a `sqlite3*`, a
`HWND` - is declared with `Handle[Tag]`. The tag is a phantom name: nothing
declares it, and it exists only so two handle types cannot be mixed up.

```
extern "C" fn fopen(path: Handle[CStr], mode: Handle[CStr]) -> Handle[FILE]
extern "C" fn fgetc(f: Handle[FILE]) -> Int
extern "C" fn fclose(f: Handle[FILE]) -> Empty

struct Suite { }

impl Suite {
    fn run(self, f: Handle[FILE]) -> Int {
        if f == null {
            return 1
        }
        let c = fgetc(f)
        fclose(f)
        return c
    }
}
```

A handle is exactly one pointer wide and is never dereferenced from Aegis:
`f.value` is rejected with an `opaque` diagnostic, because the C side owns both
the memory and the layout. The only things you can do with one are hand it back
to an extern function, store it, test it against `null`, and compare it for
identity with `==` / `!=`. Ordering (`<`) is rejected - pointers have no order.

`null` is the null pointer. It is only meaningful where a handle is expected, so
it needs an annotation to bind:

```
let f: Handle[FILE] = null     // fine - the tag is known
let f = null                   // rejected: null needs a handle annotation
if f == null { ... }           // fine
```

Because the tag on a bare `null` is unknown, mixing is checked everywhere a
handle travels: passing a `Handle[Db]` where a `Handle[File]` is expected is a
type error, and so is `db == file`.

An extern parameter declared `out name: T` is `T*` and is filled with an
`out name` argument:

```
extern "C" fn sqlite3_open(path: Handle[CStr], out db: Handle[Db]) -> Int

let rc = sqlite3_open(path, out db)   // db: Handle[Db], bound by this call
```

The compiler allocates the slot, passes its address, and binds the callee's
write as a fresh local for the following statements. Only scalar, `Str`, and
`Handle[Tag]` out types are allowed, so the slot width is always known — plus
`out name: CStruct` for C-layout structs (the address of a fresh struct the
callee fills in).

## C-layout extern structs (`extern struct`)

`extern struct Name { f: T, ... }` declares a struct whose layout is owned by
the host C compiler — the shape from a header, not an Aegis-conceived layout:

```
extern struct Point { x: Int, y: Int }
extern struct Box { origin: Point, w: Int, h: Int }
extern struct Node { data: Int, next: Handle[Node] }
extern struct Stats { size: Int, mode: u32, mtime: Int }
```

Fields admit the C scalars (`Int`, `Float`, `Bool`, `i8..u64`, `f32`),
`Handle[T]` (raw pointers from the header, `null` for C `NULL`), and nested
extern structs; owned containers, non-extern structs, and `mut`/`pub` on fields
are compile errors. An extern struct passes **by value** as a param, **by
pointer** through `out name: T` (needed for the `struct stat*` shape), and may be
returned **by value** (a non-extern struct return is still rejected). See
[types: C-layout extern structs](types.md#c-layout-extern-structs).

An extern parameter typed `fn(A, B) -> R` is a C function pointer, and the
argument must be a closure literal whose signature matches exactly:

```
extern "C" fn watch_path(interval_ms: Int, on_change: fn(Str) -> Int) -> Int

let watcher = watch_path(250, |s: Str| 0)          // no capture
let off = 1
let board = drive_board(8, 8, |x: Int, y: Int, s: Int| off + s, 3)  // captures offset
```

Callback payloads are limited to C scalars and `Str`, and `Empty` return maps
to `void`; containers, `Handle[Tag]`, and structs in callback signatures are
rejected (the sqlite row-callback shape `fn(Handle[Void], Int, Str, Str)` needs
`Handle`/`char**` payloads, which are not yet supported). A closure passed as a
callback keeps its captures alive, so the C side can invoke it later.

## Calling Aegis from C (`export fn`)

The other direction is `export fn`: a top-level function whose name becomes a
C-callable symbol with no mangling.

```
extern "C" fn simple_multiply(a: Int, b: Int) -> Int

export fn aegis_add(a: Int, b: Int) -> Int {
    return a + b
}

export fn aegis_scale(x: Int) -> Int {
    return simple_multiply(x, 2)
}
```

Exports are restricted to C-marshalable scalars: `Int`, `Float`, `Bool`, the
sized widths `i8`..`u64` and `f32`, and `void` (a body with no `-> T` arrow).
A `String`, list, or struct parameter is a compile error — C-layout `extern
struct`s cross the *extern* boundary by value/out-param, but `export fn`
signatures stay scalar-only in v1; a struct export is still open.

Export bodies are ordinary Aegis: they may call methods and `extern "C"`
functions. Export functions are host-callable in v1, not Aegis-callable, so an
export cannot recurse into Aegis code that calls it back.

Emit a library with `--emit-lib` (static) or `--emit-dylib` (shared):

```
aegis exports.aegis --emit-lib libaegis.lib      # or libaegis.a on Linux
aegis exports.aegis --emit-dylib aegis.dll       # or libaegis.so on Linux
```

`--emit-lib` writes the Aegis object alone, so the host supplies `main` and
must also link the Aegis runtime that ships with the toolchain.

`--emit-dylib` links the runtime into the shared library itself and, on
Windows, writes the matching import library next to it (`aegis.dll` →
`aegis.lib`), so a host links against the `.lib` and loads the DLL. Neither
mode invents a default `aegis_main`; pass `--main App::run` explicitly if the
host wants a library entry point.

Both flags accept object/C inputs alongside `.aegis` sources (`-l`/`-L` apply
to `--emit-dylib`, not to a static archive, which has no link step).

## Timers and Scheduled Events

Events can be scheduled to fire after a delay using the `after` keyword:

```
struct Timer {
    mut count: Int
}

impl Timer {
    fn start(mut self) -> Int {
        emit Tick(1) after 100
        emit Tick(2) after 200
        emit Tick(3) after 300
        
        on Tick(n: Int) {
            println("tick " + str(n))
            if n >= 3 {
                println("timer suite OK")
            }
        }
        
        return 0
    }
}
```

The delay is specified in milliseconds. The runtime maintains a timer queue
and checks it on each event loop iteration. When a timer expires, the event
is moved to the main event queue for processing.

## Actors

Actors are structs whose instances run independently, driven only by message
events. Declare one with `actor`, create an instance with `spawn`, and deliver
a message with `send`. An `on` handler declared inside an actor's impl captures
the targeted instance as a mutable `self`:

```
actor Counter {
    mut value: Int
}

impl Counter {
    fn create() -> Int {
        on Bump(amount: Int) {
            self.value = self.value + amount
        }
        return 0
    }
}

struct Harness {
    mut seen: Int
}

impl Harness {
    fn run(mut self) -> Int {
        let alpha = spawn Counter { value: 0 }
        let beta = spawn Counter { value: 10 }

        send(alpha, Bump(1))
        send(beta, Bump(3))

        return 0
    }
}
```

- `spawn Name { fields }` builds an actor instance and returns an opaque
  `Actor[Name]` handle; the runtime keeps a private heap copy per instance.
- `send(handle, Event(args))` delivers the event to that exact instance; its
  payload must match the `on` handler's signature.
- A message event can only be delivered with `send`; emitting it plainly is a
  semantic error. Plain events are still emitted with `emit` (target `-1`).
- Actor handles support `==` / `!=`, and the compiler rejects `emit` of a
  message, `send` of a non-message, sending a message to the wrong actor type,
  and spawning a non-actor struct.

## Receivers

Methods take an explicit `self`. Use `mut self` to mutate fields, `self` to
read. Methods are called on values: `account.deposit(100)`. Scalar receivers
may be temporaries (`5.min(9)`, `16.0.sqrt()`, `"hi".is_hi()`); container
receivers (`List`, `Map`) must be named bindings.

A method with no return type (or an explicit `-> Empty`) returns `Empty` and
can be called as a statement: `self.skip_ws()`. To call a `mut self` method the
receiver must be a **mutable binding** — declare it `let mut c = ...`; calling
`c.mutating_method()` on a plain `let` binding is a compile error.

## Reserved words

The keyword set above is reserved: those names are always lexed as keywords and
cannot be used as identifiers (struct names, field names, variable names). For
example a field named `err` is a parse error —
`expected field name, found reserved keyword 'err'` — so spell it `error`.
(This is distinct from `state`/`transition`, which are recognized
contextually, but prefer not to reuse them either.)

## Name resolution & diagnostics

Semantic failures are reported as structured diagnostics with a category,
location, and message, e.g.:

```
semantic error [type] at 17:13: arg 0 of min: expected Int, got Str
```

# language/types

# Types & memory

## Value types

Primitives are single-slot machine values on the stack.

| Type | Example | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Int` | `42` | 64-bit signed |
| `Float` | `3.5` | f64 |
| `Bool` | `true` | |
| `Str` | `"hi"` | ARC-copyable, `+` concatenates; `String` is a synonym |
| `Empty` | - | unit type, used for side-effecting methods |
| `List[T]` | `[1, 2, 3]` | runtime-allocated buffer, ARC reference counted |
| `Map[K, V]` | `{ "a": 1 }` | keyed buffer |
| `Func(params -> result)` | `\|x: Int\| x + 1` | closure, capture-by-value |
| `Option[T]` | `some(5)` / `none` | sum type |
| `Result[T, E]` | `ok` / `err(e)` | sum type |

`String` and `Str` name the same type; both spellings are accepted in type
annotations (`List[Str]` and `List[String]` are identical).

## Opaque handles

`Handle[Tag]` is a C pointer that Aegis can hold and pass but never look
through. It is one pointer wide, like `Str`, and carries a phantom tag.

| Type | Example | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Handle[Tag]` | `Handle[FILE]` | opaque C pointer; tag is phantom, never declared |

The tag exists for type safety only: `Handle[FILE]` and `Handle[sqlite3]` are
different types, so the compiler rejects passing one where the other is
expected, or comparing them with each other. It is not resolved, not declared,
and carries no runtime cost - two handles with the same tag are the same type,
and the tag disappears once the program is compiled.

What a handle supports is deliberately tiny, because the C side owns the
memory: pass it to an `extern "C"` call, return it, store it in a local or a
struct field, compare it with `==` / `!=` (pointer identity), and test it
against `null`. Everything a raw pointer has and a safe language should not
expose is gone: `h.field` is an `opaque` error, and ordering (`h1 < h2`) is
rejected because pointers have no meaningful order.

```aegis
extern "C" fn sqlite3_open(path: Handle[CStr], db: Handle[Db]) -> Empty

struct Db { }

impl Db {
    fn close(self, h: Handle[Db]) -> Empty {
        if h == null {
            return
        }
        // ... hand h back to the C library
    }
}
```

`null` is the null pointer. Because it has no tag, it only fits where a handle
is expected, and it must be annotated to bind: `let h: Handle[Db] = null` is
fine, `let h = null` is an error. That is what keeps an untyped null from
being passed to a function expecting a different handle.

## Out params

An `extern "C"` parameter can be declared `out name: T`. It stands for `T*` on
the C side — the C callee writes a result through it — so Aegis must pass an
address, not a value. At the call site that address comes from `out name`:

```aegis
extern "C" fn sqlite3_open(path: Handle[CStr], out db: Handle[Db]) -> Int

fn open(path: Handle[CStr]) -> Handle[Db] {
    let rc = sqlite3_open(path, out db)
    if rc != 0 {
        return null
    }
    return db          // db: Handle[Db], bound by the call above
}
```

The compiler allocates a slot big enough for `T`, passes its address to the C
callee, and after the call binds `db` as a fresh local whose value is whatever
the callee wrote. `db` becomes visible to the statements *following* the call
(statement-level binding — reading it in the same statement is rejected).

Holds for scalars (the sized integer widths bind C integer pointers such as
`uint32_t*` exactly), `Str` (`char**` — a C fetch-last-error getter writes the
message Aegis opens as `Str`), and `Handle[Tag]` (`sqlite3**`).
`let seven: u32 = 7` is a valid annotated literal.

`out` is a context-sensitive marker, never a reserved word: `let mut out = ""`,
`return out`, and a method param named `out` all still parse as identifiers.
Rules enforced by the checker: a plain value cannot fill an out param, `out x`
is rejected on non-out params and on method/export-fn params, a stray `out x`
outside an extern call is rejected, out params cannot be aggregates
(`out xs: List[Int]`), and an out variable cannot be read before its call.

## C-string marshaling

A `-> Str` extern return is a C `char*` that is at best transient — valid only
until the callee's *next* call (`sqlite3_column_text` is invalidated by the next
`step`/`column_*`; `sqlite3_errmsg` by the next sqlite3 call). The compiler
copies it into an owned Aegis String the moment the call returns, and an
`out msg: Str` readback is copied the same way:

```aegis
extern "C" fn sqlite3_column_text(stmt: Handle[Stmt], i: Int) -> Str
extern "C" fn sqlite3_errmsg(db: Handle[Db]) -> Str

let title = sqlite3_column_text(stmt, 0)   // snapshot, safe after the next call
let err = sqlite3_errmsg(db)               // NULL from C reads back as ""
```

A NULL C string reads back as the empty string, so a getter that returns NULL
when there is nothing to say composes (`if err == "" { ... }`) instead of
crashing the string machinery. On the way out nothing changes: `Str` params
still cross without a copy, because Aegis strings are already NUL-terminated
buffers. When a callee may *retain* the pointer past the call or write into the
buffer, make the C side an owned copy and keep that instead.

## Function-pointer callbacks

An extern signature may declare a parameter of type `fn(...) -> R`, which is a
C function pointer. An Aegis closure marshals to a C function pointer with the
declared signature, so callback-holding C APIs are reachable directly:

```aegis
extern "C" fn watch_path(interval_ms: Int, on_change: fn(Str) -> Int) -> Int
extern "C" fn drive_board(
    cols: Int, rows: Int, cell: fn(Int, Int, Int) -> Int, ticks: Int) -> Int
```

Callback parameter and return types must be C-scalars (`Int`, `Float`, `Bool`,
the sized integer widths, `f32`; an `Empty` return maps to `void`), or `Str`.
`Str` callback params are C `char*` values that are snapshotted into owned
Aegis Strings, so the closure sees a durable owned copy.
Containers and `Handle[Tag]` are not yet allowed as callback payloads.

A callback argument must be a closure literal, and its signature must match the
declared `fn(...) -> R` exactly:

```aegis
// 0-finger closure: close over nothing
let watcher = watch_path(250, |s: Str| 0)
// captures a local; the env block rides in the registry, so later ticks see it
let ticks = 0
let done = drive_board(8, 8, |x: Int, y: Int, state: Int| ticks + state, 3)
```

(The motivating sqlite shape — `sqlite3_exec(db, sql, row_cb, arg, out err)`
with `row_cb: fn(Handle[Void], Int, Str, Str) -> Int` — needs `Handle[` and
`char**` callback payloads, which are not yet supported; scalar and `Str`
payloads already work.)

A closure passed as a callback keeps its captures alive for the rest of the
program, so a callback may fire *after* its calling statement returns —
`sqlite3_exec` row callbacks and UDFs invoked later are safe.

At the callsite the declared parameter receives a plain C function pointer.
Signatures are checked precisely — mismatches produce
`callback param N of '...': closure signature ... does not match declared ...`,
non-closure arguments are rejected (`needs a closure literal, got a value`),
and non-scalar/Str callback signatures are rejected at the declaration
(`C callback parameter types must be scalars ... or Str, got ...`).

## C-layout extern structs

`extern struct` declares a struct whose layout is dictated by C, not by Aegis —
the shape from a C header (`struct stat`, win32 structs), usable directly across
the extern boundary:

```aegis
extern struct Point { x: Int, y: Int }
extern struct Node { data: Int, next: Handle[Node] }
extern struct Stats { size: Int, mode: u32, mtime: Int }
```

Fields are limited to C-as-Aegis data: the C scalars (`Int`, `Float`, `Bool`,
`i8..u64`, `f32`), `Handle[T]`, and nested extern structs. Owned containers and
non-extern Aegis structs are rejected, as are `mut`/`pub` on fields (raw C
memory is always writable). Layout follows the host C compiler's natural packing
so the Aegis declaration and the C struct agree byte-for-byte; on Windows `long`
is 32-bit, so host code should use `long long` for Aegis `Int` fields.

An extern struct crosses the boundary **by value** as a parameter, or
**by pointer** through an `out` slot, which is the `Point*`/`struct stat*` the C
callee writes:

```aegis
extern "C" fn pnt_sum(a: Point, b: Point) -> Int
extern "C" fn pnt_mul(out p: Point, k: Int) -> Empty
// p is a fresh Point*; C fills it, and p.x/p.y read back from the struct
pnt_mul(out p, 10)
```

An extern function may also **return** an extern struct by value, using the
same convention the platform uses for any C struct of that size. The result
binds like any struct local:

```aegis
extern "C" fn pnt_make(x: Int, y: Int) -> Point
let p = pnt_make(30, 4)   // p.x == 30, p.y == 4
```

A non-extern Aegis struct may **not** be returned by value (its layout is
compiler-defined); give the extern function an `out` param instead — the
diagnostic says which type and why. Pointer fields from real headers (e.g.
`struct _Node* next`) are declared as `Handle[Tag]` fields, which ride raw in the
struct and let `null` stand for C `NULL`.

## Sized numeric widths

Beyond the i64 `Int` / f64 `Float` defaults, the compiler provides the sized
widths used at FFI and systems boundaries:

| Type | C equivalent | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `i8` / `i16` / `i32` | `int8_t` / `int16_t` / `int32_t` | signed, wraps on overflow |
| `u8` / `u16` / `u32` / `u64` | `uint8_t` / `uint16_t` / `uint32_t` / `uint64_t` | unsigned; `<`/`<=`/`>`/`>=` and `/`/`%` use unsigned semantics |
| `f32` | `float` | single-precision float |

Sized values are native widths at struct fields, method parameters/returns, and
`extern "C"` signatures — so a C function taking `uint32_t` binds exactly, with
no widening shim. Inside containers (List/Map) and event payloads they are
converted to and from the container element slot.

Literals coerce ergonomically: `let x: u32 = 5` and `c + 1` (a bare integer
literal adopts the other operand's width). Between sized types and the i64/f64
defaults, conversion is explicit via the numeric conversion methods on any
numeric receiver:

```aegis
let a: i8 = 127
let b: i16 = -300
let c: u32 = 4000000000
let d: f32 = 1.5
let narrow = b.to_i8()      // truncates: -300 -> -44 (wraps)
let widen   = a.to_i64()    // 127
let u       = c.to_u64()    // 4000000000
let f64     = d.to_f64()    // 1.5 as f64
let f32     = f64.to_f32()  // back to f32
```

`to_int`/`to_float` (with `to_i64`/`to_f64` aliases) convert to the i64/f64
defaults; `to_i8()..to_u64()/to_f32()` convert to a sized width. Arithmetic
between two different widths is an error unless one side is a bare literal —
convert explicitly otherwise.

## User sum types (enums)

`enum` declares a first-class sum type with named variants; each variant may
carry up to four payload fields (or none):

```aegis
enum Shape {
    Circle(Float),
    Rect(Float, Float),
    Empty,
}
```

Values are built with the variant path, exactly like a `State::Variant`:

```aegis
let c = Shape::Circle(2.0)
let r = Shape::Rect(3.0, 4.0)
let e = Shape::Empty
```

A `match` dispatches on the discriminant and binds payloads; the compiler
**proves coverage** — every variant must be handled (or a `_` catch-all arm
must exist):

```aegis
match s {
    Shape::Circle(radius) => { /* radius: Float */ }
    Shape::Rect(w, h)      => { /* w, h: Float */ }
    Shape::Empty           => { }
}
```

Missing a variant is a compile error: `non-exhaustive match on 'Shape':
missing Rect`. Variant arity and payload types are checked at construction
(`variant 'Shape::Circle' expects 1 payload argument, got 2`).

An enum-typed payload can itself be matched directly in the pattern — a nested
variant chain (`Outer::A(Inner::B(x))`) binds the inner payload and dispatches
on both discriminants; `_` in a payload slot is a wildcard, and a plain-name
bind (`Kind::Pair(inner)`) binds the whole inner enum. Coverage extends one
level: breaking a payload into nested variants requires covering all of them
(see *Nested enum patterns* in the control-flow docs).

## Containers

`List`, `Map`, and `String` are reference counted. Copies share their storage
until it is mutated, so passing or storing a container is cheap; the language
level value semantics are preserved automatically.

## Memory & aliasing

- Stack-by-default: locals live on the call stack.
- Escape is inferred: values the compiler cannot keep on the stack become
  ARC pointers automatically. There is no `Box` or `Rc` spelling.
- There are **no nulls**. Optionality is modeled with `Option[T]`; the
  compiler tracks unhandled `Option`/`Result` values as an error.
- `mut` is visible to the compiler: assigning through an immutable binding is
  a compile error, as is mutating a list through an immutable binding
  (`xs.pop()` requires a `mut` list).

# language/control-flow

# Control flow

## Branches

```aegis
if cond { ... } else { ... }
```

`else if` chains are supported and are printed back canonically:

```aegis
if n >= 90 {
    grade = "A"
} else if n >= 80 {
    grade = "B"
} else {
    grade = "F"
}
```

The parser desugars `else if` into a nested `else { if ... }`; the deterministic
formatter recognises that shape and emits `else if` again, so formatting stays
idempotent.

Conditions must be `Bool`; a non-`Bool` condition is a type error.

## Block scope

Every block — an `if`/`else` branch, a `loop` body, and a `match` arm — is its
own scope. A `let` declared inside a block is visible only within that block:

```aegis
if ready {
    let batch = [1, 2, 3]
    println(str(batch.length()))   // ok: 3
}
println(str(batch.length()))       // semantic error [name]: undefined variable 'batch'
```

A block may re-declare (shadow) a name from an enclosing scope. The inner
binding is used inside the block and the outer binding is restored after it:

```aegis
let xs = [1, 2]
if flag {
    let xs = [1, 2, 3, 4]
    // xs.length() == 4 here
}
// xs.length() == 2 again
```

Container locals (`List`, `Map`, closures) declared in a block are released at
the end of that block — and on `break`, `continue`, or `return` out of it — so
per-iteration allocations inside a loop or branch do not leak.

## The single loop

There are no `for(i=0;...)` loops. Iteration and repetition use the keyword
`loop`:

```aegis
loop item in items { ... }   // iteration
loop { ... }                 // infinite; requires break
```

`break` and `continue` are available.

`loop c in s` also walks a `Str` one character at a time, binding `c` to a
fresh single-character `Str` each iteration:

```aegis
loop c in "a b" {
    if c == " " {
        // space
    }
}
```

Individual characters are also reachable with `s[i]`, which yields a
single-character `Str`. The loop pairs naturally with `match` on the
single-char binding (`"0" => ...`, `_ => ...`).

### Map iteration

`loop (k, v) in m` iterates a map's entries, binding the key to `k` and the
value to `v` each iteration:

```aegis
let scores = {"alice": 10, "bob": 7}
let mut total = 0
loop (name, score) in scores {
    total = total + score
}
```

`k` gets the map's key type and `v` its value type. Iterating something that
is not a `Map` is a type error (`loop (k, v) iterates a Map, got List(Int)`).
Entries arrive in hash-bucket order, which is unspecified — check aggregate
properties or key membership, not any particular sequence.

### Pair views over lists

`loop (k, v) in xs.enumerate()` walks a list in order, binding `k` to the
running index (`Int`) and `v` to each element:

```aegis
let xs = ["a", "b", "c"]
let mut out = ""
loop (i, x) in xs.enumerate() {
    out = out + str(i) + x
}
```

`loop (k, v) in xs.zip(ys)` walks two lists in lockstep, binding `k` to `xs[i]`
and `v` to `ys[i]`, stopping at the shorter list:

```aegis
loop (a, b) in xs.zip(ys) {
    // a from xs, b from ys
}
```

`enumerate()`/`zip()` are pair *views*, not first-class values — they are only
valid as the direct iterable of a `loop (k, v) in`; anywhere else they are
unknown methods (`no method 'enumerate' on type List(Int)`). Using them over a
non-list is a type error (`enumerate() requires a List`, `zip() requires two
Lists`).

### User iteration protocol

Any struct with a `next(mut self) -> Option[T]` method can be the iterable of
`loop item in x`. The method shape is the protocol, whether `next` is declared
directly or via a trait:

```aegis
struct Range2 {
    mut lo: Int,
    hi: Int,
}

impl Range2 {
    fn next(mut self) -> Option[Int] {
        self.lo = self.lo + 1
        if self.lo >= self.hi {
            return none
        }
        return some(self.lo)
    }
}

let mut r = Range2 { lo: 0, hi: 4 }
let mut total = 0
loop x in r {
    total = total + x
}
```

The loop materializes the iterable into a mutable slot and calls `next()` each
iteration, binding the `some` payload to the item and exiting on `none`.
`break`/`continue` work normally. Iterating a type without `next` is a type
error (`loop item in requires a List, String, or a type with a next() ->
Option[T]`).

## match

Sum types destructure with `match`. Every arm is `pattern => { ... }` — the
body is a statement block and there are no commas between arms:

```aegis
match r {
    ok(v) => {
        println(str(v))
    }
    err(e) => {
        println("failed")
    }
}
```

`|` joins alternative patterns in one arm (`1 | 2 | 3 => { ... }`). `_` is
the catch-all wildcard, usable only as the whole pattern of an arm — it
cannot appear inside a constructor pattern (`err(_)` is not accepted; bind
the field as `err(e)` and ignore `e`). Patterns cover the error
constructors: `ok(v)` / `err(e)` for `Result[T, E]` and `some(v)` / `none`
for `Option[T]`. The compiler rejects unhandled `Result`/`Option`
scrutinees; `?` propagates them.

### Pattern depth

An arm may carry a **guard** — a Bool expression evaluated after the pattern
matches, with the arm's bindings in scope; a failed guard falls through to the
next arm:

```aegis
match n {
    x if x < 0 => { return "neg" }
    x if x == 0 => { return "zero" }
    _ => { return "other" }
}
```

**Range patterns** match a half-open interval over an `Int` scrutinee:

```aegis
match n {
    0..10 => { /* 0 <= n < 10 */ }
    10..20 => { /* 10 <= n < 20 */ }
    _ => { }
}
```

`|` alternatives may each carry their own payload bindings, dispatched into a
shared body — every alternative's variant counts toward the exhaustiveness
check:

```aegis
match k {
    Kind::Int(n) | Kind::Nil => { return 5 }
    Kind::Str(s) => { return s.length() }
}
```

### Nested enum patterns

A variant payload that is itself an enum can be matched directly — the inner
payload binds through the two discriminants:

```aegis
match k {
    Kind::Pair(Kind::Int(m)) => { return m }        // inner payload binds m
    Kind::Pair(Kind::Nil) => { return 0 }           // nested unit variant
    Kind::Pair(_) => { return 1 }                   // `_` wildcard payload
    Kind::Int(n) => { return n }
    Kind::Nil => { return -1 }
}
```

A plain-name payload bind (`Kind::Pair(inner)`) still binds the whole inner
enum, which can then be matched separately. Guards can reference nested payload
names (`Kind::Pair(Kind::Int(m)) if m > 10 =>`). Exhaustiveness extends one
level: when a payload is broken out into nested variants, all of its variants
must be covered too — `Kind::Pair(Kind::Int(n))` alone reports
`non-exhaustive match on 'Kind': missing Pair, Nil inside Pair::Kind`. A `_` or
plain-name payload bind counts as a catch-all for the inner enum.

## Errors as values

Functions signal failure by returning `Result[T, Error]` (or `Option`). A
`?` propagates the error out of the enclosing function; otherwise a returned
`Result`/`Option` must be destructured before the program is accepted.

`ok`, `err`, `some`, and `none` are expressions (a payload is optional, so a
bare `ok` is valid). A method that returns nothing — no return type, or an
explicit `-> Empty` — must use a bare `return`; `return ok` is only valid when
the method's return type is a `Result`.

# language/contracts

# Design by contract

Contracts are first-class: every function may declare a precondition and a
postcondition. The compiler carries them into the generated binary, which checks
them at runtime. A violated contract aborts with a diagnostic such as:

```
AEGIS ASSERT FAILED: BankAccount.deposit: requires failed
```

```aegis
impl BankAccount {
    requires amount > 0
    ensures self.balance == old(self.balance) + amount
    fn deposit(mut self, amount: Int) -> Result[Empty, Error] {
        self.balance = self.balance + amount
        return ok
    }
}
```

`old(expr)` inside an `ensures` clause is evaluated before the body runs and
substituted into the postcondition, which is checked after the body. This
turns "what must be true here and now" into something the runtime can verify,
which is especially valuable for machine-and-human co-authoring: the contract
is executable documentation.

Contracts are also used at the call boundary inside the standard library to
express invariants that callers must respect, e.g. `Stack.pop` requires
`!self.is_empty()`.

# language/events

# Events & state machines

## Actor-style events

Concurrency is the actor model; there are no mutexes or semaphores. Structs
communicate by emitting and receiving events:

```aegis
emit DomainEvent.Action(payload)
```

```aegis
on DomainEvent.Action(payload) {
    // handle payload
}
```

The runtime event loop dispatches emitted events to `on` handlers; emit/on
round-trips are exercised by the test suite.

## Native state machines

`state` declares a set of named variants; an `impl` can be pinned to a state
with `impl X @ State::Variant`. Transition methods are only legal in the
guarded context, and `self.transition(State::Next)` moves the instance.

```aegis
state OrderState { Pending, Paid, Shipped }

struct Order { }

impl Order @ OrderState::Pending {
    fn process_payment(mut self) {
        // ... logic ...
        self.transition(OrderState::Paid)
    }
}
```

This is Aegis's answer to temporal bugs: "which state is this object in?" is a
compile-time fact, not a field the developer can forget to maintain.

# language/closures

# Closures & higher-order methods

Lambdas are the expression form `|param: T| expr` and the block form
`|x: T| { ... }`. They are annotated as `Func(params -> result)` where stored
in a typed binding:

```aegis
let inc = |n: Int| n + 1          // Func(Int -> Int)
```

Closures **capture by value** from the enclosing scope: scalars (`Int`, `Float`,
`Bool`) and containers — `List`, `Map`, `String`. One-pointer values
capture like scalars too: a `Handle[T]`, or another closure value (`Func`),
whose nested environment is retained by the capturing env and ARC-released when
the closure is freed. A captured
container is ARC-retained into the closure's environment block and released when
the closure is freed, so captured data stays alive for the closure's lifetime
and is cleaned up after. Capturing a `self` or a `Named` struct is a semantic
error.

A closure body may call anything the surrounding function can: methods on
captured or constructed values, compiler builtins (`print`, `str`, ...), and
`extern "C"` functions. Function names are lowered to direct calls — they are
never captured, so a closure that uses `println` or an extern fn needs no extra
slots.

```aegis
let reader = |x: Int| h_counter_get(c) + x   // captures the handle, calls an extern
let twice = |x: Int| step(step(x))           // captures the closure value `step`
```

```aegis
let rank = {"a": 3, "b": 1, "c": 2}
let names = ["a", "b", "c"]
let ordered = names.sort(|x, y| rank.get_or(x, 0) - rank.get_or(y, 0))
```

A sort comparator (or any `map`/`filter`/`fold` predicate) may read a captured
map or list — the pipeline is a filter -> map -> fold over a captured map with
no index bookkeeping.

## Nested closures

A lambda may be defined inside another lambda's body. The inner closure reads
the outer closure's params, locals, and captures out of the enclosing scope at
definition time; what it needs that neither binder set covers becomes a
*transitive* capture of the outer closure. Currying works directly:

```aegis
let add = |a: Int| |b: Int| a + b
let add5 = add(5)         // a closure
let r = add5(3)           // 8
add(5)(3)                 // also 8 — any Func-typed expression is callable
```

A block-bodied closure with no `-> Ret` annotation infers its return type from
its `return <expr>`, so a closure that returns a closure types correctly:

```aegis
let mk = |offset: Int| {
    let inner = |x: Int| offset + x
    return inner
}
mk(10)(2)                 // 12
```

## Higher-order list methods

`List[T]` has first-class HOFs, lowered to C-runtime callbacks:

| Method | Signature | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `map(f)` | `List[T].map(Func(T -> U)) -> List[U]` | transform each element |
| `filter(p)` | `List[T].filter(Func(T -> Bool)) -> List[T]` | keep where true |
| `fold(init, f)` | `fold(Func(B -> T -> B)) -> B` | left fold |
| `sort(lt)` | `List[T].sort(Func(T -> Bool)) -> List[T]` | stable sort by predicate |

```aegis
let evens = xs.filter(|x| x % 2 == 0)
let doubled = evens.map(|x| x * 2)
let total = doubled.fold(0, |acc: Int, x| acc + x)
```

`map`/`filter`/`fold`/`sort` return new lists; the input list is not mutated.
HOF predicates must return `Bool` and match the closure arity, both enforced
semantically.

# stdlib/math

# Int & Float math

## Numeric conversions

There is no implicit cast (and no `as` operator) between numeric types.
Conversion is an explicit method on the sealed builtin:

| Receiver | Method | Returns | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `Int` | `to_float()` | `Float` | exact for values in range |
| `Float` | `to_int()` | `Int` | truncates toward zero |

```aegis
let f = 3.to_float()     // 3.0
let n = 3.9.to_int()     // 3
let m = (-3.9).to_int()  // -3
```

## Compiler builtins

These dispatch to the runtime's math helpers (like `libm`), because the
operation has no source-level expression:

| Receiver | Method | Returns | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `Float` | `floor()` | `Float` | largest integer `<= self` |
| `Float` | `ceil()` | `Float` | smallest integer `>= self` |
| `Float` | `trunc()` | `Float` | round toward zero |
| `Float` | `round()` | `Float` | nearest integer, halves away from zero |
| `Float` | `sqrt()` | `Float` | |
| `Float` | `pow(e)` | `Float` | `self` raised to `e`; `e` must be a `Float` |
| `Float` | `sin()` / `cos()` / `tan()` | `Float` | argument in radians |
| `Float` | `log()` / `log10()` / `exp()` | `Float` | natural / base-10 / `e^x` |
| `Float` | `format(digits)` | `Str` | fixed-decimal (`%.*f`) with `digits` places |
| `Int` | `pad(width)` | `Str` | zero-padded decimal, right-aligned to `width` |

```aegis
let a = 16.0.sqrt()     // 4.0
let b = 2.75.floor()    // 2.0
let c = 2.5.round()     // 3.0
let d = 2.0.pow(10.0)   // 1024.0
let e = (1.0).log()     // 0.0
let g = 3.14159.format(2) // "3.14"
let h = 42.pad(5)         // "00042"
```

`format`/`pad` produce text; use them where a value must be printed with
fixed decimals or zero-padded width (interpolation format specifiers —
`"{x:.2f}"`, `"{i:05d}"` — cover the same need inline).

Argument types are checked like any other method, so `(2.0).pow(3)` (an `Int`
exponent) is rejected with `pow exponent must be a Float, got Int`. Use
`3.to_float()` when the exponent is an integer value. The `**` operator is
sugar for these: `a ** b` desugars to `a.pow(b)` (right-associative, so
`2 ** 3 ** 2` is `2 ** (3 ** 2)`).

`String.to_float()` (see [string](string.md)) is the parsing counterpart: it
returns `Result[Float, Str]` and, together with `Float.to_int()`, gives a full
text -> number -> text path now that no C shim is needed.

## Aegis seed methods (`stdlib/mathstr.aegis`)

`impl Float`, `impl Int`, and `impl String` are **sealed builtins**: they may
only be implemented in the standard library, and by-value semantics apply
(`self` is not a reference).

```aegis
impl Int {
    fn min(self, o: Int) -> Int { if self < o { return self } return o }
    fn max(self, o: Int) -> Int { if self > o { return self } return o }
    fn abs(self) -> Int         { if self < 0 { return -self } return self }
    requires e >= 0
    fn pow(self, e: Int) -> Int { let mut r = 1; loop k in 0..e { r = r * self }; return r }
}
impl Float {
    fn min(self, o: Float) -> Float { if self < o { return self } return o }
    fn max(self, o: Float) -> Float { if self > o { return self } return o }
    fn abs(self) -> Float           { if self < 0.0 { return -self } return self }
}
impl String {
    fn starts_with(self, p: String) -> Bool { ... }
    fn ends_with(self, p: String) -> Bool   { ... }
    fn contains(self, sub: String) -> Bool  { ... }
}
```

Because these are ordinary methods on the sealed targets, the compiler
type-checks each argument the same way it checks any method:
`5.min("boom")` fails with `arg 0 of min: expected Int, got Str`.
Calling them on temporaries is supported: `5.min(9)`, `16.0.sqrt()`.

Integer `Int.pow` is a real Aegis method (it needs no runtime helper), unlike
`Float.pow` which must go through `libm`. The seed module is only in scope when
`stdlib/mathstr.aegis` is among the compiler inputs — the stdlib is not
auto-loaded.


# stdlib/string

# String operations

`String` (spelled `Str` in type annotations) is an ARC-copied immutable
string. `+` concatenates; `==` / `!=` compare by content. Individual
characters are reached with a `loop c in s` iteration, which binds `c` to a
single-character `Str` (see [control flow](../language/control-flow.md)).

## Interpolation

A string literal can embed `{expr}` holes that are evaluated and stringified
at run time:

```aegis
let n = 42
let msg = "score: {n} of {n + 1}"   // "score: 42 of 43"
let who = "world"
println("hello {who}")              // "hello world"
```

Only str()-able scalar holes are allowed — `Int`, `Float`, `Bool`, and
`String`. Containers are rejected with
`interpolated values must be str()-able scalars or String, got List(Int)`.
Literal braces are written `\{` and `\}` (an unescaped `{` always starts a
hole). Interpolation is preserved by the formatter (`--fmt`).

### Format specifiers

A hole may carry a format specifier after a `:`:

```
{expr:[[fill]align][width][.precision][type]}
```

- `align`: `<` (left), `>` (right), `^` (center). Numbers default right,
  strings left.
- `fill`: a single character before the align mark (e.g. `0>8`); a `0`-prefixed
  width (`05`) is zero-padding shorthand for right-aligned numbers.
- `width`: minimum field width in characters.
- `.precision`: decimal places for a Float (`f`), or significant digits for `g`.
- `type`: `f` fixed-point Float (`%f`), `d` decimal Int, `s` String, `g` the
  general `str(Float)` form (the default).

```aegis
let x = 3.14159
let i = 42
"{x:.2f}"      // "3.14"
"{x:>10.2f}"   // "      3.14"
"{i:05d}"      // "00042"
"{i:>6}"       // "    42"
```

The type must match the value: `"{i:.2f}"` on an `Int` is a semantic error
(`format spec type 'f' requires a Float, got Int`). The spec is preserved by the
formatter (`--fmt`).
For fixed-decimal or padded output outside interpolation, `Float.format(digits)`
and `Int.pad(width)` are compiler builtins:

## Compiler builtins

| Method | Returns | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `length()` | `Int` | byte length |
| `trim()` | `Str` | new string with leading/trailing ASCII whitespace removed |
| `split(delim)` | `List[Str]` | split on a delimiter; empty delim => one whole-string piece; `""` => one empty piece |
| `to_upper()` | `Str` | ASCII uppercase mapping (fresh copy) |
| `to_lower()` | `Str` | ASCII lowercase mapping (fresh copy) |
| `repeat(n)` | `Str` | the string repeated `n` times; empty when `n <= 0` |
| `to_float()` | `Result[Float, Str]` | parse a full float literal; `err` on empty/junk/overflow |

```aegis
let s = "  a,b,c  "
let t = s.trim()            // "a,b,c"
let parts = t.split(",")    // List[Str] ["a","b","c"]
let joined = parts.join("|") // "a|b|c"
let up = "abc".to_upper()   // "ABC"
let bang = "ha".repeat(3)   // "hahaha"
```

`trim`/`split` allocate: `trim` returns a `Str`, `split` returns a
`List[Str]`. Both are compiler builtins because they need substring
construction there is no source primitive for. They validate their arguments
semantically: `s.split(42)` reports
`split delimiter must be a String, got Int`.

## Sealed `impl String` methods

`starts_with` / `ends_with` / `contains` are defined as ordinary methods on
the sealed builtin target in `stdlib/mathstr.aegis` and compose with the
builtins above. `List[Str].join(separator)` produces a string from the
elements; the separator must be a `String`.

`String.to_int()` is also a sealed `impl String` method in
`stdlib/mathstr.aegis`. It parses a signed decimal integer and returns
`Result[Int, String]`: `"42".to_int()` is `ok(42)`, `"-17".to_int()` is
`ok(-17)`, and empty input or a non-digit character yields `err(...)`. This
is the primitive for argv parsing with `argc()` / `arg(i)`.

### Slicing, search and padding

| Method | Returns | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `index_of(sub)` | `Int` | first index of `sub`, or `-1` when absent; `""` yields `0` |
| `substring(start, end)` | `Str` | half-open `[start, end)`; `requires 0 <= start <= end <= length` |
| `replace(from, to)` | `Str` | every non-overlapping `from`; empty `from` returns self |
| `is_digit()` | `Bool` | one-char `"0"`..`"9"` |
| `is_alpha()` | `Bool` | one-char ASCII letter |
| `is_space()` | `Bool` | space, `\t`, `\n`, or `\r` |
| `pad_left(width, fill)` | `Str` | left-pad with `fill` toward `width` (no-op once wide enough) |
| `pad_right(width, fill)` | `Str` | right-pad with `fill` toward `width` |

```aegis
let w = "hello world"
w.index_of("world")       // 6
w.substring(0, 5)         // "hello"
w.replace("o", "0")       // "hell0 w0rld"
"7".pad_left(3, "0")      // "007"
"7".is_digit()            // true
```

These are ordinary Aegis methods built from char indexing and `+`. There is
still no source-level substring primitive, so `substring` concatenates one
character at a time.

## Map operations

`Map` is a native hash container with the following builtins:

| Method | Requires | Returns | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `length()` | - | `Int` | |
| `contains(k)` | - | `Bool` | |
| `insert(k, v)` | `mut` map | `Int` | upserts, returns new length |
| `remove(k)` | `mut` map | `Bool` | `true` if key was present, `false` if absent |

# stdlib/list

# List operations

`List[T]` is a grow-only runtime buffer with ARC reference counting. A list
value (`{ i64 len, ptr handle }`) stays small; the handle owns the storage.

## Compiler builtins

| Method | Requires | Returns | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `length()` | - | `Int` | current logical length |
| `append(v)` | `mut` list | `Int` | append, returns new length |
| `insert(idx, v)` | `mut` list | - | insert at index |
| `get(idx)` | - | element | `xs[idx]` indexing is equivalent |
| `pop()` | `mut` list | element | remove + return the last element |
| `contains(x)` | - | `Bool` | whether an element equal to `x` is present |
| `index_of(x)` | - | `Int` | index of first match, `-1` when absent |
| `reverse()` | - | `List[T]` | fresh reversed copy (original untouched) |
| `dedupe()` | - | `List[T]` | fresh copy with duplicates removed, keeping the first occurrence |
| `slice(a, b)` | - | `List[T]` | fresh copy of the half-open range `[a, b)`, clamped to `[0, len]` |
| `map(f)` | - | `List[U]` | see [closures](../language/closures.md) |
| `filter(p)` | - | `List[T]` | predicates must be `Func(T -> Bool)` |
| `fold(init, f)` | - | `B` | left fold |
| `sort(lt)` | - | `List[T]` | new sorted list |
| `join(sep)` | `T = Str` | `Str` | join string elements |

`append` and `pop` require a **mutable** receiver (a `mut` binding). Calling
`pop()` on an immutable list is a compile error:
`pop requires mutable list 'xs'`.

`dedupe()` compares elements by slot, so it removes duplicate `Int`/`Bool`/
`Handle` values by value and `String` elements by identity (two distinct but
equal strings are both kept). It returns a fresh list and leaves the receiver
untouched.

## Composite receivers

`map`/`filter`/`fold`/`sort` (and any list-valued method result) must be
bound to a named variable before further method calls - the receiver of a
chain like `xs.map(f).length()` must be a plain identifier, matching the
"temp receivers are scalars only" rule. Bind intermediates instead:

```aegis
let ys = xs.map(|x| x * 2)
let n = ys.length()
```

## Empty lists

`[]` type-checks as `List[Any]` and is assignable to any `List[T]` field or
binding, so collection structs can start from `mut items: List[Int]` with an
empty initializer - the `types_compatible` rule recurses into element types.

# stdlib/collections

# Collections

Beyond the builtin containers, the standard library ships seed collections
written in Aegis itself under `stdlib/`. Each is generic: `Stack[T]`, `Set[T]`,
`Queue[T]`, `Deque[T]` have one concrete implementation per element type
(`Stack[Int]` and `Stack[String]` are separate); one generic source serves every
element type.

## Stack (`stdlib/stack.aegis`)

```aegis
struct Stack[T] { mut items: List[T] }

impl Stack[T] {
    fn push(mut self, v: T) -> Empty
    requires !self.is_empty()
    fn pop(mut self) -> T
    requires !self.is_empty()
    fn peek(self) -> T
    fn is_empty(self) -> Bool
    fn len(self) -> Int
}
```

`push`/`pop` are O(1) over the list-backed buffer (`pop` uses the native
`List.pop()`). `peek` and `pop` are guarded by a `requires` contract, so a
program that pops an empty stack aborts with the requires diagnostic at
runtime.

```aegis
let s = Stack[Int] { items: [] }
s.push(10)
s.push(20)
let top = s.pop()        // 20
let n = s.len()          // 1

let names = Stack[String] { items: [] }
names.push("aegis")
names.pop()              // "aegis"
```

## Set (`stdlib/set.aegis`)

A `Map`-backed set of elements. `Map.remove` is a native builtin (see
[String operations](string.md)), so `remove` on a missing key returns `false`
rather than aborting. v1 `Map` keys support `Int`, `Bool`, and `String`, so
`Set[T]` instantiates for those element types only.

```aegis
struct Set[T] { mut data: Map[T, Int] }

impl Set[T] {
    fn add(mut self, v: T) -> Empty
    fn remove(mut self, v: T) -> Bool  // false if absent
    fn contains(self, v: T) -> Bool
    fn is_empty(self) -> Bool
    fn len(self) -> Int
}
```

```aegis
let s = Set[Int] { data: {} }
s.add(10)
s.add(10)          // no-op, still length 1
s.contains(10)     // true
```

## Queue (`stdlib/queue.aegis`)

A FIFO queue backed by a grow-only `List` with a `head` index. `pop`/`peek`
are guarded by `requires !self.is_empty()`.

```aegis
struct Queue[T] { mut items: List[T], mut head: Int, mut len: Int }

impl Queue[T] {
    fn push(mut self, v: T) -> Empty
    requires !self.is_empty()
    fn pop(mut self) -> T
    requires !self.is_empty()
    fn peek(self) -> T
    fn is_empty(self) -> Bool
    fn len(self) -> Int
}
```

```aegis
let q = Queue[Int] { items: [], head: 0, len: 0 }
q.push(5)
q.push(6)
q.pop()            // 5 (FIFO order)
```

## Deque (`stdlib/deque.aegis`)

A double-ended queue implemented as two grow-only `List` stacks: `front` holds
its elements reversed (live element at the end) and `back` holds them in order.
`push`/`pop` at either end are amortized O(1) — when one side empties, the other
is reversed into it (`List.reverse()` is a native builtin). `peek` never mutates:
it reads the far element of whichever side is populated. All four end operations
are guarded by `requires !self.is_empty()`.

```aegis
struct Deque[T] { mut front: List[T], mut back: List[T] }

impl Deque[T] {
    fn push_front(mut self, v: T) -> Empty
    fn push_back(mut self, v: T) -> Empty
    requires !self.is_empty()
    fn pop_front(mut self) -> T
    requires !self.is_empty()
    fn pop_back(mut self) -> T
    requires !self.is_empty()
    fn peek_front(self) -> T
    requires !self.is_empty()
    fn peek_back(self) -> T
    fn is_empty(self) -> Bool
    fn len(self) -> Int
}
```

```aegis
let d = Deque[Int] { front: [], back: [] }
d.push_back(2)
d.push_front(1)
d.peek_front()     // 1
d.peek_back()      // 2
d.pop_front()      // 1
d.pop_back()       // 2
```

## Map enumeration (`keys` / `values` / `get_or`)

The native `Map[K, V]` provides a non-aborting lookup and entry
enumeration, so maps can be traversed without knowing the keys in advance:

| Method | Returns | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `get_or(k, default)` | `V` | the value, or `default` when `k` is absent (unlike `m[k]`, which aborts) |
| `keys()` | `List[K]` | fresh list of the live keys (hash order) |
| `values()` | `List[V]` | fresh list of the live values, matching `keys()` order |

```aegis
let mut m = {"a": 1, "b": 2, "c": 3}
let ks = m.keys()
let vs = m.values()
let mut total = 0
loop v in vs {
    total = total + v
}
let hit = m.get_or("a", 0)      // 1
let miss = m.get_or("z", -1)    // -1
```

`keys()` / `values()` allocate, so (like other list-valued results) bind the
result to a name before calling further methods on it.

## Generic impls

The `impl Stack[T]` blocks above are templates: the compiler expands one
concrete impl per used instantiation (`Stack[Int]`, `Stack[String]`, ...),
substituting the struct's type parameters in the method signatures and bodies.
The type arguments in the impl must be the struct's own parameter names
(`impl Stack[T]` for `struct Stack[T]`); an impl pinning concrete types
(`impl Container[Int]`) remains a hand-written impl on that one instantiation.
An arity mismatch (`impl Stack[Int, String]`) is a compile error.

## Roadmap

JSON pretty-printing and a richer string formatter are still on the way.
Struct-keyed maps are deliberately out of scope: structs are mutable, so a
mutated key would invalidate its hash slot — encode composite keys as a
`String` instead. See [Roadmap](../roadmap.md).


# stdlib/json

# JSON

`stdlib/json.aegis` is a self-contained RFC 8259 JSON implementation written
in Aegis on top of compiler builtins (no C). It features a recursive-descent
parser with precise error messages, a compact serializer, and typed accessors
that return `Option`/`Result` instead of aborting.

A parsed document is a `Json` enum value:

```aegis
enum Json {
    Null,
    Bool(Bool),
    Num(Float),
    Str(String),
    Arr(List[Json]),
    Obj(Map[String, Json]),
}
```

`Null`, `Bool`, `Num`, `Str` are scalars; `Arr`/`Obj` carry container payloads.
Because a container can hold enum values, a `List[Json]` or
`Map[String, Json]` can store *any* JSON value, including nested arrays and
objects.

## Parsing

`JsonParser` is stateless; construct one and call `parse`:

```aegis
let jp = JsonParser {}
match jp.parse(text) {
    ok(j)  => { /* use j */ }
    err(m) => { println(m) }
}
```

`parse` returns `Result[Json, Str]`. The parser:

- skips whitespace between tokens;
- decodes the literal escapes `\" \\ \/ \n \t \r` plus `\uXXXX` for those same
  code points (`\u0022 \u005c \u002f \u000a \u0009 \u000d`) and `\u0000`;
- rejects anything else: a `\uXXXX` for an unsupported code point, an unknown
  escape (`\b`, `\f` ...), a leading zero, a mangled number, a trailing
  non-whitespace character, or a structural mistake — each with a message that
  names the offending construct.

```aegis
let jp = JsonParser {}
let r = jp.parse("{\"a\":[1,2.5,null],\"b\":\"hi\\nthere\"}")
```

## Inspection

`type_of(j)` names the variant (`"null"`, `"bool"`, `"num"`, `"str"`, `"arr"`,
`"obj"`). The typed accessors return `Option` and yield `none` on a variant
mismatch instead of aborting:

| Method | Returns | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `is_null(j)` | `Bool` | true for `Json::Null` |
| `as_bool(j)` | `Option[Bool]` | |
| `as_float(j)` | `Option[Float]` | |
| `as_int(j)` | `Option[Int]` | whole `Num`s only (`f == f.floor()`) |
| `as_str(j)` | `Option[String]` | decoded string value |
| `as_arr(j)` | `Option[List[Json]]` | |
| `as_obj(j)` | `Option[Map[String, Json]]` | |
| `get(j, key)` | `Option[Json]` | `Obj` member by key (no abort on missing) |
| `at(j, i)` | `Option[Json]` | `Arr` element by index (bounds-checked) |

```aegis
match jp.as_int(item) {
    some(n) => { total = total + n }
    none    => { /* not a whole number */ }
}
let name = jp.get(person, "name")
```

## Serialization

`to_string(j)` produces compact JSON (`{"a":[1,2],"b":null}` — no whitespace).
`quote(s)` renders a `String` as a `"..."` literal with `\"`, `\\`, `\n`,
`\t`, `\r` escapes, so object keys and string values round-trip. `Num` values
are written with `str(f)`.

```aegis
let s = jp.to_string(doc)     // "{\"y\":true,\"z\":null,\"s\":\"hi\n\"}"
```

## Round-trip

The self-test suite exercises parse/stringify round-trips, error paths, and
container typed accessors. Because a `Map` iterates in hash order, only
*same-key-set* round-trips are asserted to be deterministic.

## Roadmap

The parser intentionally targets the RFC 8259 core. The roadmap calls for
indentation control in `to_string`, full `\uXXXX` code point decoding, and a
`parse_file` convenience over the IO stdlib. See [Roadmap](../roadmap.md).

# stdlib/csv-table

# CSV & tables

`stdlib/csv.aegis` and `stdlib/table.aegis` are self-contained text-formatting
modules written in Aegis on top of compiler builtins (no C). Both compile
standalone and are covered by their self-test suites.

## CSV (`stdlib/csv.aegis`)

`Csv` encodes and decodes an RFC 4180 subset. A table is a `List[List[Str]]` —
rows of fields — which needs no new runtime support (`List` of `List` of `Str`
is an ordinary nested container).

| Method | Returns | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `parse(text)` | `List[List[Str]]` | split into records and fields |
| `encode(rows)` | `Str` | serialize, quoting only fields that need it |

```aegis
let csv = Csv {}
let rows = csv.parse("name,note\nalice,\"x, y\"\n")
let back = csv.encode(rows)   // "name,note\nalice,\"x, y\"\n"
```

`parse` follows the small RFC:

- a field may be double-quoted to embed a comma, a quote, or a newline;
- a doubled quote (`""`) decodes to a literal `"`;
- records end at `\n` or `\r\n` (a lone `\r` is dropped);
- a trailing newline does not create an empty final record, and blank input
  yields no rows.

`encode` quotes a field only when it contains a comma, quote, CR, or LF, and
doubles any embedded quote. For canonical input, `encode(parse(t)) == t`.

## Tables (`stdlib/table.aegis`)

`Table.render(headers, rows)` turns a header `List[Str]` and a `List[List[Str]]`
into a fixed-width text table: each column is padded to the widest of its header
and cells, the header is underlined with a dash rule, and short rows pad their
missing trailing cells.

```aegis
let t = Table {}
let table = t.render(["Name", "Age"], [["Al", "7"], ["Bea", "12"]])
// Name | Age
// -----+----
// Al   | 7
// Bea  | 12
```

Padding is built from `String.repeat` (`s + " ".repeat(width - s.length())`),
so the module stays standalone and does not depend on `stdlib/mathstr.aegis`.

## Round-trip

The self-test suites exercise quoted fields, CRLF and LF records, the
trailing-newline rule, blank input, encode round-trips, and table alignment.


# stdlib/io

# File IO & stdin

These are value-level compiler builtins (like `print` / `argc`). Failures are values: `read_file`, `read_line`, and
`list_dir` return `Result[String, String]` / `Result[List[String], String]`, and
`write_file` returns `Result[Int, String]` (bytes written). Files are
read/written as raw bytes; `read_line` is the only operation that strips a
newline.

| Function | Returns | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `read_file(path)` | `Result[Str, Str]` | whole file; `err` when it cannot be opened/read |
| `write_file(path, content)` | `Result[Int, Str]` | bytes written; `err` on failure |
| `file_exists(path)` | `Bool` | |
| `read_line()` | `Result[Str, Str]` | one line from stdin, trailing newline stripped; `err` at EOF |
| `list_dir(path)` | `Result[List[Str], Str]` | entry names of a directory (unsorted, `.`/`..` omitted); `err` when it cannot be opened |

```aegis
match read_file("notes.txt") {
    ok(text) => { println(text) }
    err(why) => { println("read failed: " + why) }
}
match write_file("out.txt", "hello\n") {
    ok(n) => { println(str(n) + " bytes") }
    err(why) => { println(why) }
}
match list_dir("src") {
    ok(entries) => {
        let mut i = 0
        while i < entries.length() {
            println(entries[i])
            i = i + 1
        }
    }
    err(why) => { println(why) }
}
```

Paths are ordinary `String`s; the separator is not abstracted
(`"C:/tmp/a.txt"` and `"dir/file"` both work). The argument type is checked:
`read_file(42)` fails with `read_file path must be a String, got Int`, and
`list_dir(42)` fails with `list_dir path must be a String, got Int`.

`list_dir` returns leaf entry names (not full paths) and does not distinguish
files from subdirectories; inspecting an entry further is a job for
`file_exists` or a subsequent `list_dir`. It is implemented per-platform in the
runtime (`FindFirstFileA` on Windows, `readdir` elsewhere).

A `match` on a `Result` binds its payload by reference, so a bound `String`
supports the full string surface. The test suite verifies these behaviors
against scratch files and directories, including the `err` path on a missing
file.

The stdlib is not auto-loaded: these IO builtins need no `import`, but
seed-module methods (for example `String.replace`) require
`stdlib/mathstr.aegis` among the compiler inputs.


# stdlib/time-rand

# Time & randomness

Value-level compiler builtins (like `print` / `argc`).

| Function | Returns | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `now_ms()` | `Int` | monotonic milliseconds since an arbitrary epoch (for elapsed time, not wall-clock dates) |
| `rand_seed(n)` | `Empty` | seed the PRNG; `0` restores the built-in default seed |
| `rand_int(lo, hi)` | `Int` | uniform in the half-open range `[lo, hi)`; returns `lo` when `hi <= lo` |
| `rand_float()` | `Float` | uniform in `[0.0, 1.0)` |

```aegis
rand_seed(42)
let die = rand_int(1, 7)          // 1..=6
let p = rand_float()              // 0.0 <= p < 1.0

let t0 = now_ms()
// ... work ...
let elapsed = now_ms() - t0
```

The generator is a deterministic `xorshift64*`: seeding with the same value
reproduces the same sequence, which is what makes tests (and save/replay
scenarios) stable. `now_ms` reuses the same monotonic clock the event-timer
queue already uses, so it never jumps backwards on a clock adjustment.

Argument types are checked: `rand_int("a", 3)` fails with
`rand_int bounds must be Ints, got Str`. Verified by
The test suite verifies reproducibility, range invariants, and clock
monotonicity.


# stdlib/hashing

# Hashing

`hash(x)` is a value-level compiler builtin (like `now_ms` / `argc`). It maps a
scalar or string to a deterministic, non-negative `Int` using FNV-1a (64-bit) —
the same family the `Map` uses for its string keys.

| Function | Returns | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `hash(s)` | `Int` | FNV-1a over the string's bytes; `hash("")` is defined |
| `hash(n)` | `Int` | FNV-1a over the 8 little-endian bytes of the `Int` |
| `hash(b)` | `Int` | `hash(true)` / `hash(false)`, i.e. `hash` of `1` / `0` |

```aegis
let a = hash("hello")     // deterministic across runs
let b = hash(42)
let c = hash(true)
```

Properties:

- **Deterministic.** The same input always yields the same value, across runs
  and machines — no per-process seed.
- **Non-negative.** The 64-bit result is masked to 63 bits, so it is safe to
  use directly as `hash(x) % n` without sign pitfalls.
- **Not cryptographic.** This is a fast content hash for buckets, tables and
  fingerprints, not a password or integrity primitive.

Verified by the `hash` checks in the builtin test suites.


# stdlib/net

# Net

Minimal blocking TCP for backend servers, over the runtime's socket helpers
(Windows Winsock / POSIX). Connections and listeners are
opaque `Handle[T]` values; user code only ever passes them back to the `Net`
methods.

Aegis has no free functions, so TCP hangs off one instance:

```aegis
let net = Net {}
if net.init() != 0 {
    println("winsock init failed")
}
let l = net.listen("127.0.0.1", 8080)
if l == null { /* bind/listen failed */ }
let conn = net.accept(l)   // blocking accept
```

| Method | Returns | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `init()` | `Int` | WSACleanup-safe WSAStartup once; 0 on success. Call before any other method. |
| `listen(host, port)` | `Handle[TcpListener]` | bind + listen; `null` on failure; empty host binds `INADDR_ANY` |
| `port(listener)` | `Int` | the actual bound port (needed after port 0) |
| `accept(listener)` | `Handle[TcpConn]` | blocking; `null` when the listener died |
| `connect(host, port)` | `Handle[TcpConn]` | dial out; `null` on failure |
| `recv(conn, max)` | `Str` | up to `max` bytes; `""` means EOF or error |
| `send(conn, data)` | `Int` | bytes written; short count or `-1` means the peer went away |
| `close_conn(conn)` | | release a connection handle |
| `close_listener(listener)` | | release a listener handle |

## Hostnames and DNS

`host` is either a numeric IPv4 or a hostname. Resolution inside the runtime
tries `inet_pton` first (no resolver round trip for `127.0.0.1`) and falls back
to `getaddrinfo(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM)`, so `net.connect("api.example.com", 80)`
works like `net.connect("127.0.0.1", 80)`. IPv6 is not handled yet; the
resolver asks for `AF_INET` only.

## Port 0

`listen(host, 0)` asks the OS for an ephemeral port; read it back with
`port(listener)` before blocking in `accept`. This is what makes a one-process
smoke test deterministic: the caller can print the real port for a client to
dial.

## Blocking and ownership

Everything is synchronous - one connection at a time, no threads. Handles are
opaque: they must not be stored in containers crossing the FFI boundary, and are
closed explicitly. `recv` returning `""` is the caller's stop signal (EOF and
error share the channel). The externs are declared in `stdlib/net.aegis`; the module compiles standalone with
compiler builtins only.

# stdlib/http

# HTTP

A minimal HTTP/1.1 server built on `stdlib/net.aegis`. `serve` blocks in an
accept loop and dispatches each connection to a `fn(Request) -> Response`
handler, so routing is ordinary Aegis code (match on `req.path`).

```aegis
let http = Http {}
fn handler(self) -> fn(Request) -> Response {
    return |req: Request| -> Response {
        let h = Http {}
        if req.path == "/" {
            return h.respond_ok("webapp ok")
        }
        return h.respond_404()
    }
}
let rc = http.serve(8080, handler())
```

| Type | Fields |
| --- | --- |
| `Request` | `method: Str`, `path: Str`, `headers: Map[Str, Str]`, `body: Str` |
| `Response` | `status: Int`, `headers: Map[Str, Str]`, `body: Str` |

| Method | Returns | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `respond_ok(body)` | `Response` | status 200, empty headers |
| `respond_404()` | `Response` | status 404, `"not found"` |
| `respond_400()` | `Response` | status 400, `"bad request"` |
| `with_header(r, name, value)` | `Response` | copy `r` with one more header |
| `respond_json(body)` | `Response` | status 200 with `Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8` |
| `serve_on(net, listener, handler)` | `Int` | answer exactly one connection on a pre-bound listener, then release it |
| `serve(port, handler)` | `Int` | listen on `127.0.0.1` and answer connections until the listener dies |

`serve_on` splits out the bind so the caller can pick an ephemeral port, read it
back with `net.port(l)`, and publish it before blocking in `accept` - the shape
The router is exercised for deterministic behavior.

## Response headers

`response_text` serializes the custom `headers` map first (hash-bucket order),
then emits `Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8` only when no
`content-type` key is present (matched case-insensitively), and finally forces
`Content-Length` (computed from the body) and `Connection: close`. Header names
keep their case; lookups on `Request.headers` are case-sensitive, and a
duplicate request header collapses to the last value. Custom
`Content-Length`/`Connection` entries cannot be overridden.

## Request parsing

`parse_request` splits the raw bytes on the first blank line
(`"\r\n\r\n"`), parses the header lines into `Request.headers` (a
`Map[Str, Str]`), and sets `path` to include the query string (split on `?`
yourself). Reads stop at the header terminator or the 64 KiB cap
(`read_request`), which covers GET and POST-with-body; there is no chunked
encoding or keep-alive, and every response sets `Connection: close`. A
malformed request is reported as a `Request` whose `method` is `""` (check with
`is_valid`) - v1 cannot carry a struct inside `Option[...]`, so the empty
sentinel is the error channel rather than `none`.

## Constraints

Single-threaded: one connection is handled to completion before the next
`accept`. `serve` binds `127.0.0.1` (use `net.listen` + `serve_on` for other
bind addresses). The stdlib is not auto-loaded: splice `http.aegis` (and
`net.aegis`) into the compilation ahead of your program.

# quickstart

# Quickstart

Aegis ships as a self-contained compiler toolchain. You install a release,
point it at a C compiler for the final link step, and compile `.aegis` programs
to native executables.

## Install

**Windows (x64):**

```powershell
irm https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Sockney89/aegis-dist/main/install.ps1 | iex
```

**Linux (x86_64):**

```sh
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Sockney89/aegis-dist/main/install.sh | sh
```

Both installers download the latest release, verify its SHA-256 checksum, and
install to a per-user directory (`%LOCALAPPDATA%\Aegis` on Windows, `~/.aegis`
on Linux), adding the `bin/` to your `PATH`. Pin a version with `-Version 0.1.0`
(PowerShell) or `--version 0.1.0` (shell). On Windows you can also use Scoop:

```
scoop bucket add aegis https://github.com/Sockney89/aegis-dist
scoop install aegis
```

## Link step: a C compiler
